analysis.one_liner: Requires asbestos bankruptcy trusts to publish quarterly reports naming every claimant and payment.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 221-199 in November 2013 on a near party-line vote, but the Senate never acted and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies facing thousands of asbestos lawsuits often go through bankruptcy and set up a trust that pays sick claimants on the company's behalf. This bill would force those trusts to file public quarterly reports listing each person who files a claim, their exposure history, and what they were paid. Supporters called it fraud prevention; opponents said it would expose dying workers' private claim information and hand asbestos companies a tool to contest and slow down legitimate claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Asbestos defendant corporations and their insurers. The public reports would give them detailed data on who is claiming what, which they could use to challenge claims in court and press insurers to offset liability, reducing what they ultimately pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asbestos defendant corporations and their insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends federal bankruptcy law to require every trust set up under bankruptcy code section 524(g) to file quarterly reports on the court's public docket describing each claim it received, the claimant's name and exposure history, and the basis for any payment [S2][S4].

It also requires the trusts, on written request, to turn over information about payments and claims to any party to any lawsuit involving asbestos liability — which in practice means the companies and insurers defending those suits [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: People with asbestos-related disease filing trust claims. Their names, exposure histories, and settlement amounts would become public court records, and the trusts — funded by the bankrupt companies for victims — would bear the cost of quarterly reporting, which can slow payments to people who are often seriously ill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick asbestos claimants and their trusts

drawbacks.text: The public reports would list each claimant's name and exposure history on a public docket, raising privacy concerns for people with fatal illnesses and creating a database opponents said defendants could use to discourage or contest claims [S2][S4].
The trusts would bear the administrative cost of preparing and publishing detailed quarterly reports on every claim, an expense drawn from assets set aside to compensate victims [S2][S4].

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill was that public reporting would expose inflated or duplicate claims and deter fraud against the trusts; supporters pointed out the reports would exclude confidential medical records and full Social Security numbers [S2][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency benefit is real but narrow: bankruptcy courts and parties to trust proceedings already have access to claim information, so the main change is making it public and handing a copy to any asbestos-liability defendant or insurer who asks. The costs fall on a small population of seriously ill claimants — loss of privacy, plus reporting overhead that comes out of funds meant to pay them — while the clearest beneficiary is the corporate defense side. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge the bill's practical effect would be to make trust claims harder and slower to pursue.

outcome.mechanism: It squeaked through the House on a mostly party-line vote, went to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill by a 17-14 vote in October 2013, and it reached the floor in November under a rule allowing only pre-printed amendments [S6].

Before final passage, Democrats offered a motion to send the bill back with an amendment exempting veterans and service members from the disclosure requirements and requiring their asbestos claims to be paid before death; it failed 197-224, with no Republicans voting for it [S6][S7].
The House passed the bill 221-199 on November 13, 2013, with 216 of 230 Republicans voting yes and only 5 of 200 Democrats [S6][S8].
The Senate received the bill on November 14, 2013, and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action was taken for the rest of the 113th Congress [S1][S4][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos victims and the trusts that pay them came out ahead of the bill's supporters' goals, since the public reporting requirement never took effect. Asbestos defendant corporations and insurers did not gain the claim-by-claim database the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos claimants; corporate defendants got no new tool

for.name: Rep. Blake Farenthold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through committee and floor action.

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee on a 17-14 vote and managed its floor consideration under a rule limiting amendments to a pre-approved list.

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and asbestos defendant companies
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for the bill as a transparency and anti-fraud measure.

against.name: Rep. Bill Owens
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to recommit the bill with instructions to exempt veterans and service members from the disclosure rules and ensure their claims are paid before death; it failed 197-224.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in November 2013 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Asbestos victims' advocacy groups and plaintiffs' attorneys
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would publicize sick claimants' information and help companies contest legitimate claims.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost exactly by party: 216 of 230 Republicans voted yes and 192 of 200 Democrats voted no, with just 5 Democrats crossing over and 7 Republicans defecting [S8].

industries.note: The bill would have handed these companies public, claim-by-claim data from the trusts, which they could use to contest claims and slow payouts to sick workers. Their gain would come directly at the cost of the people exposed to their products.
Insurers that share asbestos liability with bankrupt companies would get the same reports and could use them to dispute or reduce their reimbursement obligations, lowering their payouts.
Claimants would see their names, exposure histories, and payment amounts published quarterly, and the trusts would absorb reporting costs that reduce the funds available to pay them.
